techniques.name: Basic Step
techniques.tagline: The foundation — 6 steps, two sets of 3
techniques.what: The On2 basic step is the heartbeat of NY-style salsa. You step on counts 1-2-3 and 5-6-7, with a natural pause (break) on counts 4 and 8. That gives you exactly 6 steps per 8-count phrase. Leaders step forward on 1, followers step back on 1. If you find yourself taking more than 6 steps, you are losing the count — reset and simplify.

Step back with left foot, returning toward center

Step back with right foot (leader) or forward (follower)
Step in place or shift weight to left foot
Step forward with right foot, returning toward center

arm_styling.action: Arms relaxed at sides or in partner frame; no exaggerated movement
Mirror the opposite side; keep elbows soft and close to body

instructor_quotes: Count 1-2-3-5-6-7 for a basic step. That's 6 steps total. If you're stepping more, you're losing time and the count.
There's a break between each set of 3 counts: 1-2-3 (break) 5-6-7 (break). Use these breaks to reset and stay on time.
Followers: don't change your basic step when the leader starts going back with their left foot. Keep your normal pattern until the lead signals otherwise.

techniques.drill: Stand alone without music. Say '1-2-3-BREAK-5-6-7-BREAK' out loud while stepping. Do this for 2 full minutes until the pause feels natural. Then add music at half speed.
techniques.common_error: Taking 8 steps instead of 6 — students add an extra step on the break counts (4 and 8). If your feet are always moving, you are never resetting. Force yourself to pause and feel the break.

techniques.name: Prep Step
techniques.tagline: Twist right to unlock the left turn
techniques.what: The prep step is the setup move that signals an upcoming turn. Before a left (inside) turn, you twist your body to the right on counts 1-2. This rightward twist 'loads' your body like a spring — when you release on count 3, you naturally unwind into the left turn. Without the prep, the turn feels forced and off-balance. Think of it as a conversation with your body: twist right first, then the left turn becomes effortless.

techniques.common_error: Skipping the twist entirely and just stepping forward. Without the rightward body rotation on count 2, the left turn has no momentum and you will feel stuck or have to muscle through it.

techniques.name: Inside Turn (Left Turn)
techniques.tagline: Turn on 3, face forward on 6, style with intention
techniques.what: The inside turn (also called the left turn or traveling left) is the first turn beginners learn in NY On2. The leader signals the turn through the prep step and arm lift; the follower pivots off their right foot on count 3 and completes the rotation to face forward by count 6. The arm styling — keeping your right arm close to your ear and tracing your body from behind your neck down through count 7 — is what separates a clean turn from a sloppy one. Every movement should be deliberate, not tentative.

techniques.name: Suzy Q
techniques.tagline: Cross, step, cross — tight, twisted, intentional
techniques.what: The Suzy Q is a solo shine (footwork pattern) done in place. The pattern is cross-step-cross: your back foot crosses behind your front foot, you step to the side, then cross again. The key is keeping your back foot CLOSE behind your front foot — you are not passing your front foot, you are staying tight and controlled. Add hip twist for styling: the visual effect of the Suzy Q comes from the hip rotation, not from how wide your legs go. You can prep the Suzy Q by lifting your right leg on counts 5-6-7-1 before starting the pattern.

techniques.name: Cross Body Lead
techniques.tagline: Guide your follow across your body — assertive, compact, clear
techniques.what: The cross body lead (CBL) is the most fundamental partnered move in NY-style salsa. The leader steps forward on 1, then on count 2 adds a subtle hip twist and arm signal to guide the follower across their body. The follower pivots off their right foot while their left foot swings to the left. Leaders: do NOT step into your follow's space — keep a normal forward step and use body language and touch to communicate direction. Keep your arms at shoulder width around their head — compact, not wide. Followers: keep your right elbow down to maintain frame, and pivot cleanly off your right foot.

hard_transitions.why: Students often miss the prep entirely because it happens within the basic step — it looks like a basic step but the body twist on count 2 is the signal. If you don't feel the rightward coil loading, you have skipped the prep and the turn will feel forced.

The turn initiates on count 3, which is the THIRD beat of the first set — students often turn too early (on 2) or too late (on 5). The prep twist on 2 must be complete before the pivot begins on 3. Rushing this transition causes the turn to be off-axis.

After the turn, students are often disoriented and lose the count. The Suzy Q starts on count 1 of the next phrase. You must land from the turn, face forward on 6, do the weight-shift-only on 7, and then immediately begin the cross on 1. There is no extra step to recover — you must be ready.

After the quarter beats (stepping only on odd counts 5 and 7), students must return to the full basic step pattern. The rhythm feels different coming out of quarter beats — you are going from sparse stepping back to 6 steps per phrase. Count out loud to stay on time.

techniques.name: Basic Step
techniques.tagline: The foundation of everything — anchor your 3 and your 7
techniques.what: The On2 basic step is an 8-count pattern split into two halves. Counts 1-2-3 travel forward (or lead forward), with count 3 as a planted anchor. techniques.name: Suzy Q
techniques.tagline: Cross in front, pick up your leg, say it as you do it
techniques.what: The Suzy Q is a salsa shine (solo footwork) built on a repeating cross-step-cross pattern. The critical rule is that you ALWAYS cross in front of your standing foot — never behind. The verbal pattern 'cross, step, cross' helps you execute it correctly. After each cross, pick up your leg to prepare for the next movement — don't drag your foot. The circular Suzy Q adds a directional rotation, turning to face four walls (bathroom, wall, door, mirror) as you complete each repetition.

mechanics.action: Cross your right foot in FRONT of your left foot — never behind.
Step your left foot out to the side (the 'step' in 'cross-step-cross').
Cross your right foot in FRONT again — pick up your leg after to prepare.
Cross your left foot in FRONT of your right foot to begin the reverse direction.
Step your right foot out to the side.
Cross your left foot in FRONT again — pick up your leg to prepare for the next rep.

arm_styling.action: Arms can swing naturally opposite to the crossing foot, or be held in a relaxed salsa frame. Keep them low — no big gestures.
As you rotate through the four directions, let your arms follow the body's rotation naturally. Don't force them — connection and simplicity.

instructor_quotes: Always cross in front of your foot, whether crossing over left or right—never behind. This is the standard for Suzy Q.
Say the pattern aloud as you move: 'cross, step, cross, cross, step, cross.' Saying it helps you execute it correctly.
Pick up your leg after the cross to prepare for the next step—don't drag your foot.
For circular Suzy Q, think of four directions: bathroom, wall, door, and mirror.
Create smooth curves and circles rather than sharp corners when transitioning between directions in circular Suzy Q.
You can reverse the circular Suzy Q by starting with your left foot and going to the right instead of left.
If you struggle with Suzy Q, practice Suzy Q in isolation before attempting the full combo.
Great dancing is made of connection and simplicity, not complex movements.

techniques.name: Inside Turn (Right Turn)
techniques.tagline: Start on 6, land on 8, keep it low and snatch — don't present
techniques.what: The inside turn (also called the right turn or traveling left turn in NY On2) is a partner move where the follower turns to their right under the leader's raised arm. The leader signals the turn by raising their hand on count 1, the follower begins turning on count 2, and the turn completes by count 6-7. The critical timing rule: the follower starts turning on count 6, not before. After the turn, land on count 8 (a pause), then continue with 1-2-3. The hand connection stays right-to-right throughout.

mechanics.action: Leader raises hand to signal the turn — arm goes up on count 1 to prepare the follower.
Follower turns to the RIGHT on count 2. Leader guides them to the right.
Follower commits to the turn — start turning on count 6, not before. Don't hesitate.
Keep your 7 AWAY from your partner, not toward them. This creates space.
LAND on count 8 — this is a pause. Don't rush into the next count.
Continue with the basic step after landing. Maintain right-to-right hand hold throughout.

arm_styling.action: Raise your arm LOW — don't reach high. Keep the arm low and grab low to maintain control.
Use your ELBOW to activate the switch, not your hands. Keep your arm straight and use elbow engagement.
Snatch the hand — don't present it slowly. Quick, decisive hand movement prevents the follower from reaching for the wrong hand.

instructor_quotes: Start turning on count 6, not before. Don't hesitate—commit to the turn at 6.
The follower turns to the right on count 2. As the leader, raise your hand on count 1 to signal the turn, and guide them to the right.
Keep your 7 away from your partner, not toward them. This creates space and prevents stepping on each other.
Don't reach high to grab your partner's hand during a turn. Keep your arm low and grab low to maintain control.
Use your elbows to activate the switch, not your hands. Keep your arm straight and use elbow engagement to signal the hand switch.
Don't present your hand slowly—snatch it. Quick, decisive hand movement prevents the follower from reaching for the wrong hand.
After turning on 6, land on count 8 (a pause), then continue with counts 1, 2, 3. Don't rush the landing.
Maintain right-to-right hand hold throughout the turn and transition.

techniques.drill: With a partner: practice ONLY the hand raise signal on count 1, then the follower turn on count 2, stopping there. Repeat 8 times until the signal is automatic. Finally, practice the landing on count 8 by counting aloud: '6-turn, 7-space, 8-LAND, 1-2-3.'
techniques.common_error: Starting the turn too early (before count 6) or rushing through the landing on count 8. Leaders also commonly reach too high with their arm and push with their hand instead of using elbow activation. techniques.name: Transition Back to Basic
techniques.tagline: Land on 8, pause, then flow into 1-2-3
techniques.what: After any turn or shine, returning cleanly to the basic step requires a specific landing protocol. You land on count 8 — this is a deliberate pause, not a rushed step. From that landing, you flow naturally into counts 1-2-3 of the next basic. The right-to-right hand hold is maintained throughout, so there is no hand switch needed. This transition is what makes the combo feel smooth rather than choppy.

mechanics.action: Complete the turn or shine movement — this is the last active count of the previous move.
Keep your 7 away from your partner — create space, don't crowd.
LAND — this is a pause. Plant your foot, absorb the weight, breathe.
Flow into the basic step. Don't rush — let the 8 breathe before you go.

arm_styling.action: Arms settle back to basic frame position during the landing pause.
Resume normal basic step arm position — low, relaxed, connected.

instructor_quotes: After turning on 6, land on count 8 (a pause), then continue with counts 1, 2, 3. Don't rush the landing.

techniques.common_error: Rushing from the turn directly into count 1 without landing on count 8. This causes the basic step to start on the wrong count and throws off the partnership timing for the rest of the song.

hard_transitions.note: The circular Suzy Q starts from basic but adds rotation — students often lose the count when adding the turn. The cross-step-cross pattern must stay tight while turning to face each wall.
Around the world is a half-rotation that follows the circular Suzy Q. Students confuse which direction to go because they just finished turning. Anchor on counts 3 and 7 — these feet stay planted.
After rotating moves, students are disoriented and step on wrong counts. Return to basic by finding count 1 and stepping forward (leader) — the anchor on 3 and 7 resets your orientation.
Transitioning from solo shines to partner work requires re-establishing connection. Leaders must be assertive with direction — snatch the hand, dont present it. Keep it low.

techniques.name: Basic Step (Around the World)
techniques.tagline: A circular, full-360° basic that anchors your weight and travels through 12, 9, and 6 o'clock positions
techniques.what: The NY On2 basic step is the foundation of all salsa movement. In this class the instructor emphasizes executing it as a 'circular motion' — rather than stepping straight back and forward, you trace a full circle with your footwork, moving through every directional angle (12, 9, and 6 o'clock positions) so the pattern travels 'around the world.' Weight must be anchored cleanly between repetitions to maintain balance and control before initiating the next direction.

mechanics.action: Step forward (leader) or back (follower) — initiate the circular arc, weight transfers fully onto the stepping foot

Replace weight back to center, feet collect under hips

On2 break on the back step, hip drops opposite side
Replace weight, collect, ready to redirect to next angle

arm_styling.action: Arms stay relaxed and slightly rounded in front of the body; on the break (count 2) the opposite arm naturally swings forward with the hip drop
Arms mirror the opposite side; on the back break (count 6) the lead arm extends slightly to maintain frame and connection with partner

instructor_quotes: Execute the basic step with a circular motion, creating a full circle pattern with your footwork
Practice the basic step around the world by moving through all directional angles (12, 9, 6 o'clock positions)
Anchor your weight properly between basic step repetitions to maintain balance and control

techniques.drill: Stand alone facing a mirror. Mark 12, 9, and 6 o'clock positions on the floor with tape. Execute your basic step starting at 12 o'clock, then rotate your body so your next basic faces 9 o'clock, then 6 o'clock, completing the full circle. Count aloud: '1-2-3, 5-6-7' and pause on every 2 and 6 to feel the anchor. Do 3 full circles slowly, then 3 at tempo.
techniques.common_error: Stepping straight back and forward like a pendulum instead of tracing a circular arc. This kills the 'around the world' rotation and makes partner connection rigid. Think of your feet drawing a clock face on the floor, not a straight line.

techniques.name: Right Turn
techniques.tagline: A clean clockwise right turn with controlled timing, spotting, and a stable hold before the next phrase
techniques.what: The inside turn (also called the right turn or traveling left turn in NY On2) sends the follower rotating clockwise under the leader's raised arm. The leader initiates the turn on count 5 by raising the joined right hands and guiding the follower's rotation with a smooth arc overhead. The follower must spot, maintain their frame, and complete the full rotation by count 1 of the next phrase. The instructor counts through the full 8-count (5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) to ensure the turn is completed with proper timing and not rushed.

mechanics.action: Leader and follower execute basic step in open position, establishing connection and timing before the turn

instructor_quotes: Execute the right turn with clean, controlled rotation, maintaining your frame and connection

techniques.drill: With a partner, practice ONLY the turn lead on counts 5-6-7. Start in open hold. On count 5, raise your right hand slowly and guide your partner under. Freeze on count 7 and check: is your partner facing you? Is your arm back down? Is the connection re-established? Repeat 8 times slowly before adding music.
techniques.common_error: Rushing the turn by pulling the follower's arm instead of lifting it. The lead is an upward arc, not a horizontal pull. Also: dropping the arm too early (before count 7) which causes the follower to lose their rotation axis and stumble out of the turn.

hard_transitions.why: The instructor shifts from facing the mirror (solo basic) to facing the room to demonstrate the turn lead arm. Students must recognize this pivot as the transition from footwork drill to turn mechanics — the body orientation change signals a new technique is being introduced.

The instructor calls 'Lily' and moves from solo demonstration to live partner work. The energy and timing shift significantly — students must now apply what they watched to an actual partner connection. The hand-join moment (frame 017) is where many beginners lose their timing.

After the inside turn lands on count 1, the instructor immediately sets up the cross body lead. This is the hardest transition because the follower is still completing their rotation while the leader must already be opening their body to the side to create the cross body lane. Rushing this causes the follower to collide with the leader.

The 'around the world' directional change requires the dancer to redirect their circular arc between repetitions. The anchor on count 3 (frame 003) must be solid before the body can rotate to the new angle. Beginners often skip the anchor and stumble into the next direction.

sections.name: Section 1: Solo Basic Step — Circular Motion

drills.name: Stationary Basic (On2 Timing)
drills.instructions: Stand in place, no travel. Count aloud: '1-2-3, 5-6-7.' On every 2 and 6, pause for one full beat and feel your weight anchor into the floor. Do not move to the next step until you feel that anchor. Repeat 16 times.

drills.name: Around the World (3 Positions)
drills.instructions: Mark 12, 9, and 6 o'clock on the floor with tape or shoes. Execute your basic step facing 12 o'clock for 2 repetitions, then rotate your body to face 9 o'clock for 2 repetitions, then 6 o'clock for 2 repetitions. Complete 3 full circles. Focus on the anchor between each directional change — do not rush the rotation.

drills.name: Full Circle Continuous
drills.instructions: Now do the 'around the world' continuously — rotate a little bit on every anchor so that by the end of 8 repetitions you have completed a full 360°. Stay upright ('I stay upright'). Add music at 70% tempo. Do 4 full circles.

drills.name: Arm Arc Drill (No Partner)
drills.instructions: Stand alone. On count 5, raise your right arm in a smooth arc overhead — imagine you are lifting a balloon, not pulling a rope. On count 7, lower it back down. Repeat 16 times to counts '5-6-7.' The arc should be smooth and circular, not jerky.

drills.name: Solo Turn Spot
drills.instructions: Practice spotting for the inside turn. Stand in place, pick a spot on the wall in front of you. On count 5, begin rotating clockwise. Keep your eyes on that spot as long as possible, then whip your head around to find it again. Complete the rotation by count 7. Repeat 12 times.

drills.name: Full 8-Count Turn Sequence
drills.instructions: Count through the full 8-count as the instructor taught: '5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.' On counts 5-6-7 execute the turn. On counts 1-2-3 execute the basic step. On counts 4-5 prepare for the next turn. Add music at 80% tempo. Do 8 repetitions.

sections.name: Section 3: Partner Work — Basic + Inside Turn

drills.name: Slow Connection Drill
drills.instructions: With a partner, stand in open hold. Execute ONLY the basic step together for 2 minutes — no turns. Focus on matching your weight transfers. On every count 2 and 6, both partners anchor simultaneously. Feel the connection through your joined hands.

drills.name: Turn Lead Freeze Drill
drills.instructions: Leaders: on count 5, raise your arm and FREEZE. Check: is your arm making a smooth arch? Is your elbow soft? Is your partner able to step under without ducking? Followers: step under and FREEZE mid-rotation. Check: is your frame compact? Are you spotting? Resume on count 7. Repeat 8 times.

drills.name: Full Sequence: Basic + Inside Turn + Transition
drills.instructions: Execute the full sequence from class: 2 basics in open hold, then inside turn on counts 5-6-7, then 2 basics, then inside turn again. After 4 repetitions, add the cross body lead transition. Count aloud throughout. Add music at full tempo for the final 2 minutes.

key_frames.label: Starting Position
key_frames.description: The instructor's ready position — feet hip-width, weight centered, arms relaxed. Study this frame to understand the neutral posture you return to between every move. Body is upright, no tension.

key_frames.label: The Anchor (Count 2)
key_frames.description: This is the most important frame for On2 timing. The instructor's weight is fully settled on the breaking foot, hip drops, and there is a clear pause before the next step. This is what 'anchor your weight properly' looks like — freeze here and feel it.

key_frames.label: Knee Engagement
key_frames.description: The instructor demonstrates 'knee on this side now' — the knee lifts naturally as part of the circular basic step. This shows the hip-and-knee connection that gives salsa its characteristic look. The body stays upright while the lower body does the work.

key_frames.label: 6 O'Clock Position
key_frames.description: The instructor has rotated to face away from the mirror — the 6 o'clock position in the 'around the world' circular basic. This frame proves the full 360° rotation is happening. Study the foot placement and body angle.

techniques.name: Basic Step (On2)
techniques.tagline: The foundation — forward, back, switch on 2 and 6
techniques.what: The NY On2 basic step is a 6-count pattern (counts 1-2-3, 5-6-7) where you step forward on 1, break on 2, recover on 3, step back on 5, break on 6, and recover on 7. The key is landing your weight cleanly on count 2 and 6 (the 'on2' timing), bending both knees on count 7 to drop your weight onto the back foot, and switching directions smoothly between the two halves of the pattern. Keep joints relaxed and don't rush your feet.

mechanics.action: Step forward with your left foot (leader) / right foot (follower)
Break — transfer weight onto that foot; this is the 'on2' moment
Recover — bring feet together or step in place, switching direction
Step back with your right foot (leader) / left foot (follower)
Break — transfer weight onto that foot
Bend both knees and drop weight onto back foot; recover to neutral

arm_styling.action: Arms relaxed at sides or in frame; allow natural opposition swing
Maintain frame; on count 7 let arms settle as knees bend and weight drops

instructor_quotes: bend both knees
drop on the seven
switch directions
keep your joints relaxed and don't rush your feet — take your time with each count
make the transition from 6-7 to 1 smooth and deliberate

techniques.drill: Stand alone facing the mirror. Count out loud: '1-2-3, 5-6-7.' On 1, step forward. On 2, feel your weight land — this is your 'on2' moment. On 3, switch direction. On 5, step back. On 7, bend both knees and drop. Repeat for 4 minutes without music, then add music at 50% speed.
techniques.common_error: Rushing count 7 — students step through it without bending the knees or dropping the weight, making the transition into count 1 choppy and late.

techniques.name: Suzy Q
techniques.tagline: Out, step, cross — three distinct weight changes with direction switches
techniques.what: The Suzy Q is a salsa shine (solo footwork) where you execute three distinct weight changes: step out to the side, step in place, then cross your feet over cleanly while facing forward. The instructor emphasizes three separate actions — out, step, cross — with clear direction switches between each. On the cross step, you must face forward and cross your feet cleanly. It fits into the same 1-2-3 / 5-6-7 timing as the basic step.

mechanics.action: Step out to the side — open your foot outward
Step in place — transfer weight, begin rotating hips
Cross — bring the foot across cleanly, face forward, feet crossed
Step out to the other side — mirror the first half
Step in place on the other side
Cross to the other side — face forward, feet crossed cleanly

arm_styling.action: Arms can go overhead or out to sides for styling — instructor cues 'hands in the air' during the combo
Mirror the arm styling from the first half; keep shoulders relaxed and open

instructor_quotes: execute the Suzy Q as: out, step, cross — three distinct weight changes with clear direction switches

techniques.drill: Say 'out-step-cross' out loud as you do each weight change. Do it slowly first without music: step your right foot out (out), step left foot in place (step), cross right foot over left (cross). Face forward on the cross. Then reverse. Once clean, add the On2 counts: out=1, step=2, cross=3.
techniques.common_error: Turning the body on the cross step instead of keeping the chest facing forward — the cross is a foot action, not a body rotation.

techniques.name: Right Turn (Single Stationary)
techniques.tagline: Turn right on 5-6-7 (leader) or 1-2 (follower) — spot your partner early
techniques.what: The single stationary right turn is a full 360-degree turn to the right. For leaders, the turn happens on counts 5-6-7 (initiate on 5-6, complete by 7). For followers, the turn happens on counts 1-2 (initiate on 1, complete by 2). The critical teaching point is to NOT wait until the last minute — initiate the rotation early, keep your right shoulder open as you start, and spot your partner so you are facing them again by count 1 (leaders) or count 2 (followers). After the turn, your footwork pattern is: forward, forward, back, back, back, forward.

mechanics.action: Initiate the right turn — don't wait, begin rotating immediately, right shoulder opens
Mid-turn — you should be halfway through the rotation, spotting your partner
Complete the turn — land facing your partner, weight drops on back foot
Leaders: face partner by count 1 — whip through to complete rotation if needed
Followers: spot partner by count 2 — looking too late means you're not spotting properly

arm_styling.action: Right arm/shoulder opens to initiate the turn; left arm follows through the rotation
Arms return to frame or open position as you land facing your partner

don't wait till the last minute

on count 1 after a right turn, you must be facing your partner again — whip through to complete the rotation
spot your partner by count 2 (followers) or count 1 (leaders) — looking too late means you're not spotting properly

techniques.drill: Practice the right turn solo first. On counts 5-6-7, turn right. Say 'initiate-spot-land.' Your goal: be facing the mirror again by count 7 (or count 1 at the latest). Then practice with a partner: leader gives the right turn lead on 5-6, follower turns on 1-2. Both spot each other.
techniques.common_error: Waiting until count 7 to start turning — this makes the turn rushed and late, causing you to miss your spot and arrive facing the wrong direction on count 1.

techniques.name: Inside Turn (Traveling Left)
techniques.tagline: Followers turn left on 1-2-3; leaders turn left on 5-6-7
techniques.what: The inside turn (also called the traveling left turn in NY On2) is a left-turning pattern where the follower turns left on counts 1-2-3 and the leader turns left on counts 5-6-7. The follower should be facing the partner by count 2, and the leader by count 1. This is a partner-work move where the leader raises the connected hand to create a frame for the follower to turn under. The turn travels slightly forward rather than spinning in place.

Follower: mid-turn — should be facing partner by this count; spot early

Leader: mid-turn, spotting partner

techniques.drill: Leaders: practice raising your arm on count 5-6-7 of the previous basic, so the frame is ready for count 1. Followers: practice stepping forward and turning left on 1-2-3 solo, spotting an imaginary partner. Then combine: leader raises arm on 7, follower steps under on 1.
techniques.common_error: Followers completing the turn too late — arriving on count 3 instead of being fully faced by count 2, which throws off the reconnection and the next basic step.

techniques.name: Half Step
techniques.tagline: Same timing as the basic, but only turn halfway — 0.5 and 0.5
techniques.what: The half step uses the exact same On2 timing as the basic step (1-2-3, 5-6-7) but instead of completing a full directional change, you only turn halfway. The instructor describes it as '0.5 and 0.5' — half of the basic on each side. This is used as a transitional or preparatory move and helps develop body awareness of the halfway position before committing to full turns or direction changes.

mechanics.action: Execute the first half of the basic step — step, break, recover — but only rotate halfway through the direction change
Execute the second half — step, break, recover — again only halfway, mirroring the first half

arm_styling.action: Arms stay relaxed and close to the body; no full extension since the body is only halfway through
Mirror the first half; arms follow the body's half-rotation naturally

the half step to the right uses the same timing as the basic (1-2-3, 5-6-7) but you only turn halfway instead of fully

techniques.drill: Do the basic step but imagine a clock face. On a full basic, you'd face 12 o'clock, then 6 o'clock. On the half step, you only go to 3 o'clock each time. Count '1-2-3, 5-6-7' and stop at the halfway point each time. Feel the difference in body rotation.
techniques.common_error: Accidentally doing a full basic step — students forget to stop at the halfway point and complete the full rotation, losing the 'half and half' quality the instructor is building.

hard_transitions.why: The basic step ends with a back step on 5-6-7, and the Suzy Q begins with a lateral step out on 1. Students often continue the basic's forward motion instead of switching to the lateral 'out' direction of the Suzy Q. The direction change must be clean and immediate.

The turn-around requires a full 180-degree rotation of the body while maintaining the On2 timing. Students lose the count during the rotation and arrive facing the wrong direction or on the wrong beat. The Suzy Q's cross step can be used to initiate the rotation, but the timing must stay locked.

Moving from solo shines to partner hold requires finding your partner, establishing frame, and syncing your basic step — all without losing the count. Students often pause to 'find' their partner and arrive late on count 1.

The leader must raise the arm on count 7 of the basic to be ready for the follower's turn on count 1. If the arm goes up late (on count 1 or 2), the follower has no frame to turn under and the turn is missed or rushed.

hard_transitions.why: The side-to-side ends on count 3 (slow recover); the basic step begins on count 1 of the next phrase. Beginners rush the transition and lose the On2 break. Wait for the full slow on 3 before stepping forward on 1.
The turn initiates on count 1 — the same count as the forward step in the basic. Beginners often take the forward step AND then try to turn, creating a late pivot. The pivot IS the count-1 step.
After chaining right turns, the leader must re-establish the slot and frame before leading the inside turn. Rushing from the right turn directly into the CBL causes the follower to lose orientation.

The inside turn ends with the follower facing the leader; the CBL immediately sends her across. The leader must lower the hand and re-establish connection on counts 5-6-7 before the CBL begins on count 1.
After multiple CBL variations (left turn, right turn, comb), returning to closed position requires the leader to actively bring the follower in — not wait for her. The reset happens on counts 5-6-7.

techniques.name: Cross Body Lead (CBL)
techniques.tagline: One of the five fundamentals — transition from home position across the slot
techniques.what: The cross body lead moves the follower across the leader's body from one side of the slot to the other. The leader steps out of the slot on 1-2-3 to create space, then guides the follower through on 5-6-7. Proper hand positioning and frame control are essential. This is one of the five fundamental moves every leader must master.

techniques.drill: Leaders: practice the footwork alone — step back-side on 1-2-3, step forward on 5-6-7. Add a partner: focus on opening the slot cleanly on 1-2-3 before guiding on 5. Follower: walk straight through, do not turn until led.
techniques.common_error: Leader fails to fully clear the slot on 1-2-3, causing a collision. The leader must step completely out of the follower's path before count 5.

techniques.name: Comb
techniques.tagline: Palm up, elbow in — brush hair, don't rotate the frame
techniques.what: The comb is a styling/transition move where the leader raises the right arm (palm up, elbow in), brings the hand to center, then moves it up and behind the follower's neck — like brushing hair. It transitions into cross-hand position without hand-switching. The follower maintains fingertip connection throughout; the leader is responsible for disconnecting.

instructor_quotes: raise your right arm with palm up and elbow in, bring your hand to center, then move it up and behind the follower's neck

techniques.drill: Leaders: practice the arm motion alone — palm up, elbow in, arc upward and behind an imaginary neck. Say 'palm up, elbow in, brush' on each repetition. With partner: slow motion only until follower can maintain fingertip connection throughout.
techniques.common_error: Leader rotates the follower's frame instead of passing the hand behind the neck. The comb is a hand path, not a body rotation. Also: follower breaking connection anticipating the move.

hard_transitions.why: Hip walk ends on a tap (no weight), so you must confirm which foot holds weight before stepping into the basic. If you tap on the wrong foot, your basic will start on the wrong side.
Basic step uses every count (1-2-3, 5-6-7); chord beat skips even counts. The rhythm feel changes dramatically. Count aloud to avoid filling in the held beats.
Chord beat ends on an odd count; domino hip walk must start with the correct foot. Track your weight at the end of chord beat — start domino hip walk with the opposite foot.
Transitioning from solo to partner requires establishing frame and connection before the first count. Leaders must offer hand on 5-6-7 prep so both partners are synchronized on count 1.
CBL ends with follower on opposite side; comb must begin immediately on the next 1-2-3. Leader must switch to right hand connection during CBL completion to set up the comb arm path.

drills.name: Hip Walk — Eyes Up
drills.instructions: Mark hip walk without music. Say 'step, tap, step' aloud. Look RIGHT when stepping right, LEFT when stepping left. Never look down. 4 reps each direction. Add music at 50% speed.

drills.name: Chord Beat — Odd Counts Only
drills.instructions: Clap on 1-3-5-7 only for 2 bars. Then walk one step per clap. Say '1-hold-3-hold-5-hold-7-hold.' After 4 bars, check weight foot. Start next sequence with opposite foot.

drills.name: Domino Hip Walk
drills.instructions: With a partner or mirror: one person starts hip walk on count 1, second person starts on count 3 (one beat offset). Maintain the offset for 4 full phrases. Switch who leads the timing.

drills.name: Right Turn — 7-1-3 Footwork
drills.instructions: Without music: say '7-1-2-3' aloud. On 7 step back, on 1 land facing mirror, on 3 step forward. 8 repetitions. Add music only after footwork is automatic.

drills.name: Left Turn — Solo then Partner
drills.instructions: Solo: 8 left turns using 7-1-3 footwork. Partner: leader raises left arm on 5-6-7 prep, follower turns on 1-2-3. Follower: maintain fingertip connection throughout. 8 reps each.

drills.name: Cross Body Lead — Slot Clearing
drills.instructions: Leaders: practice footwork alone — step back-side on 1-2-3, step forward on 5-6-7. Add partner: focus on clearing the slot completely on 1-2-3 before guiding on 5. Follower walks straight through.

drills.name: Comb — Slow Motion
drills.instructions: Leaders: practice arm motion alone — palm up, elbow in, arc upward. Say 'palm up, elbow in, brush.' With partner: slow motion only. Follower: maintain fingertip connection, do not anticipate.

drills.name: Full Combo Run
drills.instructions: Run the full sequence at tempo: Basic -> CBL -> Comb -> Basic. Focus on smooth transitions, not speed. If a transition breaks, stop and drill that transition alone for 4 reps before continuing.

techniques.name: Basic Step (On2)
techniques.tagline: The foundation: 1-2-3, 5-6-7 with real weight transfers
techniques.what: The NY On2 basic step breaks on counts 2 and 6. Leaders step forward on 1, break back on 2, replace on 3, hold 4; step back on 5, break forward on 6, replace on 7, hold 8. Every count requires a committed weight transfer — no flat or neutral standing.

Break/change of direction — leader steps back (right foot), follower steps forward (left foot). This is the On2 accent.
Replace weight in place. Hold 4.

Break forward — leader steps forward (left foot), follower steps back (right foot). Second On2 accent.
Replace weight in place. Hold 8.

arm_styling.action: Arms relaxed, elbows slightly bent. Upper body angled, not fully rotated. Hips lead the movement.
Mirror the forward/back weight shift with a subtle counter-rotation of the torso. Keep it compact.

instructor_quotes: don't be flat
step into the pivot with the opposite foot pushing off
let your hips do the talking rather than turning your whole torso
Counts 4 and 8 are held/weight-bearing counts. Don't step on 4 or 8.

techniques.drill: Stand alone, no music. Say '1-2-3, hold, 5-6-7, hold' aloud. On each count, fully commit your weight — feel the floor under your standing foot. Add hip movement only after the footwork is automatic.
techniques.common_error: Stepping on count 4 or 8, or staying flat/neutral between counts instead of committing weight on every step.

techniques.name: Right Turn (Solo & Lead/Follow)
techniques.tagline: Forward (1), turn (2), step in place (3) — keep turning, don't stop the flow
techniques.what: The right turn in NY On2 follows a 1-2-3 structure: step forward on 1, pivot/turn right on 2 (the On2 break), and step in place on 3. The key error is stopping between steps — the body must keep rotating continuously through 2-3. In partner work, the leader turns on count 6 (not 2) and raises the left arm on 7, brings it up on 1, and sends the follower on 2.

mechanics.action: Step forward (left foot for leader). Begin initiating the rightward rotation.
Pivot/turn right — this is the On2 break. Body continues rotating. Don't stop here.
Step forward (right foot) to complete the turn. Weight lands on right foot. Do NOT step back.
Leader turns on 6. Raise left arm on 7, bring up on 1, send follower on 2. Motion is in-and-out, not a straight lift.

arm_styling.action: Leader raises left arm (the whole arm, not just the hand) to frame the follower's turn.
Leader brings arm up — in-and-out motion. Turn under your arm, not under your hand.
Follower enters the turn. Leader keeps elbow lower and arm bent so follower's frame stays relaxed.
Follower holds the turn before landing — don't land immediately on 3. Hold it, then land on 4.

don't stop the flow

on count 3 of a right turn, step forward (not back)
leaders: turn on count 6 (not 2) when dancing with a partner
raise your left hand (arm, not just hand) on count 7
turn under your arm, not under your hand
hold the turn before landing
over rotate

techniques.name: Zig-Zag
techniques.tagline: Full 1-2-3, 5-6-7 — clear weight transfers, open toward the door
techniques.what: The zig-zag is a traveling pattern that opens the dancer toward the door/audience. It occupies a full 1-2-3, 5-6-7 phrase — never compressed into a half count. Each step requires a clear, committed weight transfer. The pattern alternates direction (zig then zag) with the body opening on the 1-2-3 phrase.

mechanics.action: Step diagonally forward-left (opening toward the door). Full weight transfer.
Step diagonally forward-right. On2 break direction. Full weight transfer.
Step to close or continue the diagonal. Hold 4.
Step diagonally back-right (reversing the zig). Full weight transfer.
Step diagonally back-left. On2 break. Full weight transfer.
Step to close or continue. Hold 8.

arm_styling.action: Arms travel with the body's diagonal opening. Keep upper body angled, not fully rotated.
Arms mirror the reverse diagonal. Stay compact — no wide arm swings.

instructor_quotes: The zig-zag is a full count: 1-2-3, 5-6-7. Don't rush or compress it into a half count.
Step into the zig-zag with clear weight transfers on each count. Don't skip or glide through the steps.
opening toward the door
keep it compact

frames.caption: Zig-zag opening — both dancers stepping diagonally, bodies angling toward the mirror/door.
Zig-zag mid-phrase — weight clearly on one foot, opposite foot stepping through the diagonal.
Zig-zag completing — body opened toward door, weight settled, preparing to transition.

techniques.drill: Mark the zig-zag in place first: step L-R-L (1-2-3), hold, step R-L-R (5-6-7), hold. Then add the diagonal travel. Say 'zig' on 1 and 'zag' on 5 to reinforce the full phrase timing.
techniques.common_error: Rushing the zig-zag into a half-count or gliding through steps without committing weight. The pattern must feel like six distinct steps, not a slide.

techniques.name: Suzy Q
techniques.tagline: Cross (1), step (2), cross (3) — always start with a cross
techniques.what: The Suzy Q is a crossing footwork pattern in NY On2. The pattern is: cross (1), step (2), cross (3), cross (5), step (6), cross (7). It always begins with a cross on count 1. When starting with the left foot, you must cross on 6-7 first (not step forward). The crossing foot stays slightly behind the front foot — never step out further than your front foot.

mechanics.action: Cross left foot over right (or right over left). Foot lands slightly behind the front foot.
Step to the side (uncross). Weight transfers fully.
Cross again. Same foot crosses. Hold 4.
Cross (opposite foot). Mirror of counts 1-3.
Step to the side (uncross).
Cross again. Hold 8.

arm_styling.action: Arms can frame the crossing motion — subtle counter-rotation of shoulders with each cross.
Mirror the arm styling. Keep it compact and stylized, not exaggerated.

instructor_quotes: Suzy Q always starts with a cross on count 1
cross, step, cross
keep your foot slightly behind the front foot — don't step out further than your front foot
if starting a Suzy Q with your left foot, you must cross on 6-7 first (not step forward)

frames.caption: Suzy Q entry — cross on count 1 visible, foot landing slightly behind front foot.

techniques.drill: Stand still, no music. Say 'cross, step, cross' three times slowly. Feel the foot landing slightly behind the front foot on each cross. Then add counts: 'cross (1), step (2), cross (3), hold (4), cross (5), step (6), cross (7), hold (8).'
techniques.common_error: Stepping the crossing foot out further than the front foot, or starting with a step instead of a cross. If you start with the left foot, you must cross on 6-7 first.

techniques.name: Beginner Combo
techniques.tagline: Basic → Right Turn → Zig-Zag → Right Turn → Suzy Q
techniques.what: The beginner combo chains all five techniques into one continuous phrase. The sequence is: basic step (1-2-3), right turn (5-6-7, leader turns on 6), zig-zag (1-2-3, opening toward the door), right turn (5-6-7), Suzy Q (1-2-3, 5-6-7). In partner work, the leader can switch hands during the combo — 'I switch the hands turn' — to set up the next move without breaking connection.

techniques.common_error: Losing the On2 timing between moves — especially rushing the zig-zag or landing the right turn on the wrong count. The combo only works if every transition respects the 1-2-3, 5-6-7 phrase.

hard_transitions.why: The right turn lands on count 3 (forward, not back), and the zig-zag must begin immediately on count 5 opening toward the door. If you land the turn on the wrong foot or step back on 3, you'll be on the wrong foot for the zig-zag entry.

The zig-zag closes on count 7, and the right turn begins on count 1. The body must stop traveling diagonally and redirect into the forward step of the right turn. Rushing the zig-zag's last step causes the turn to start late.

The Suzy Q must start with a cross on count 1. If the right turn doesn't complete cleanly (weight on right foot, forward), the crossing foot will be wrong and the Suzy Q will start with a step instead of a cross.
In solo, the leader turns on count 2. In partner work, the leader turns on count 6. This timing shift is the most common error when moving from solo practice to partner work.

Switching hands mid-combo requires the leader to change the connection without breaking the follower's frame or telegraphing the switch. The hand switch happens on 1-2-3 while the follower is still tracking the lead.

drills.name: Basic Step Count-Out
drills.instructions: No music. Say '1-2-3, hold, 5-6-7, hold' aloud. Fully commit weight on every count. Feel the floor under your standing foot. Add hip movement only after footwork is automatic. Never step on 4 or 8.

drills.name: Zig-Zag Isolation
drills.instructions: Mark the zig-zag in place: step L-R-L (1-2-3), hold, step R-L-R (5-6-7), hold. Then add diagonal travel. Say 'zig' on 1 and 'zag' on 5. Each step must feel distinct — no gliding.

drills.name: Suzy Q Cross Pattern
drills.instructions: Stand still. Say 'cross, step, cross' three times slowly. Feel the foot landing slightly behind the front foot on each cross. Add counts: cross (1), step (2), cross (3), hold (4), cross (5), step (6), cross (7), hold (8).

drills.name: Solo Right Turn Walk-Through
drills.instructions: Say 'forward (1), turn (2), step in place (3)' on each count. On 2, keep your body spinning — don't pause. On 3, land forward, not back. Repeat 10 times, then add music at half speed.

drills.name: Continuous Rotation Drill
drills.instructions: Practice the right turn focusing only on counts 2-3. Start the rotation on 2 and don't stop until you've completed the full turn on 3. The key phrase: 'don't stop the flow.' Do 20 repetitions.

drills.name: Leader Arm Timing (partnerwork)
drills.instructions: Without a partner, practice: raise left arm on 7, bring up on 1 (in-and-out motion), send on 2. Repeat 10 times. Then add a partner and practice without announcing the turn verbally.

drills.name: Combo Walk-Through (half speed)
drills.instructions: With a partner, walk through the full combo at half speed counting aloud: 'basic (1-2-3), turn (5-6-7), zig-zag (1-2-3), turn (5-6-7), Suzy Q (1-2-3, 5-6-7).' Leader: practice the hand switch before adding music.

drills.name: Transition Drilling
drills.instructions: Isolate the two hardest transitions: (1) right turn → zig-zag and (2) zig-zag → right turn. Run each transition 10 times at half speed, then 10 times at full speed. Focus on foot placement at the landing of each turn.

drills.name: Full Combo at Music Speed
drills.instructions: Run the full combo to music: basic → right turn → zig-zag → right turn → Suzy Q. Repeat 5 times without stopping. If you lose the timing, don't stop — find the next count 1 and re-enter.

key_frames.label: Starting Position
key_frames.description: Both dancers in starting position before the combo begins. Study the body angle, foot placement, and relaxed arm position — this is the neutral you return to between combos.

key_frames.label: Suzy Q Cross (count 1)
key_frames.description: The Suzy Q always starts with a cross on count 1. Study the foot position — the crossing foot lands slightly behind the front foot, not further out. This is the most common error point.

key_frames.label: Partner Right Turn — Follower Mid-Spin
key_frames.description: Follower mid-spin under leader's raised arm. Leader's elbow is bent and lower — 'turn under your arm, not under your hand.' Follower's frame is relaxed. Critical frame for leaders to study arm position.

key_frames.label: Follower Landing from Turn
key_frames.description: Follower landing after holding the turn. Weight lands on right foot. This is the 'hold the turn before landing' moment — the follower doesn't land immediately on count 3.

key_frames.description: Leader raising arm for the right turn in partner work. The in-and-out motion (not a straight lift) is visible. This is the correct arm path for sending the follower into a turn.

key_frames.label: Combo Hand Switch
key_frames.description: Leader switching hands mid-combo. The transition happens without breaking the follower's frame. Study how the leader's arm position changes while maintaining connection.

key_frames.label: Combo Closing — Close Connection
key_frames.description: The combo's closing move with the follower's leg hook/wrap. Both dancers in close frame. This is the 'keep it compact' principle at its most visible — no wasted space or energy.

key_frames.label: Combo Complete — Final Position
key_frames.description: Both dancers with arms raised, combo complete. Study the body positions — this is the natural end of the phrase. The crowd's reaction confirms the energy of a well-executed combo.

techniques.name: Basic Step (On2)
techniques.tagline: Foundation forward-back mambo break on counts 2 and 6
techniques.what: The NY On2 basic is a 6-step pattern across two 4-count bars. Leader breaks forward on count 2 (left foot), recovers on 3, closes on 4 (no weight); breaks back on count 6 (right foot), recovers on 7, closes on 8. The break/change-of-direction happens ON 2 and ON 6 — never on 1 or 5. Weight stays compact, knees soft, hips follow the weight transfer naturally.

techniques.name: Suzy Q
techniques.tagline: Heel-toe rocking shine with hip punctuation
techniques.what: The Suzy Q is a stationary shine (solo footwork) done in place. Both feet rock heel-toe in alternating directions — right heel drops as left toe lifts, then switch. In NY On2 context it fits into the 1-2-3 / 5-6-7 phrase. The instructor cues it after the basic, suggesting it replaces or follows a basic phrase. Hips accent each rock naturally from the weight shift.

techniques.what: After solo shines, the instructor brings partners together and introduces 'tension, hold' — a cue for maintaining elastic resistance through the handhold so leader and follower can feel each other's weight and timing. In NY On2 the connection is especially important on the break counts (2 and 6) because that is when the lead/follow signal is transmitted. 'Side basic' in partner work means the basic step done side-by-side or in open position.

hard_transitions.why: After completing the clock circuit you must re-orient to the front slot without losing the On2 timing. The pivot happens on the prep count — if you pivot late you break on the wrong count.
The Suzy Q is stationary but the entry must land on count 1 so the heel-toe rocks align with 1-2-3. Entering late puts the rocks off-phrase.
Exiting Suzy Q back to basic requires collecting your feet on count 3 or 7 so you are ready to break on the next 2 or 6. Rushing the exit causes a missed break.
Re-establishing the frame after shines must happen before the next break count. If you grab hands ON count 2 you lose the lead signal for that break.
The arm raise for the turn lead must begin on count 1 (or 5) so the follower has time to read the lead and begin her turn on 2 (or 6). Late arm raises produce rushed, off-balance turns.

techniques.name: Suzy Q
techniques.tagline: Cross-step-cross shine that travels forward in the slot
techniques.what: The Suzy Q is a NY On2 shine executed on counts 1-3 (or 5-7) after a 'core beat' setup. The footwork is cross-right, step-left, cross-right (or mirror image). Critically, the move must travel forward — not sideways or backward — so you stay connected in the slot. End with weight on the non-crossing foot so you are grounded for the next phrase.

Travel forward with the Suzy Q; do not let your crossing foot go too far to the left, right, or back, or you will create too much gap between you and your partner.
End each Suzy Q with your weight on the foot that is NOT crossing.

techniques.drill: Mark the floor with tape in a straight line. Practice Suzy Q so your crossing foot always lands on or ahead of the tape — never behind it. Say 'cross-step-cross' aloud on each count. Do 4 reps solo, then 4 reps with eyes closed to feel the weight transfer.
techniques.common_error: Letting the crossing foot drift sideways or backward, creating a gap with your partner. Keep the cross traveling forward along the slot line.

techniques.name: Right Turn
techniques.tagline: Single stationary right turn with On2 cross-step entry on 7
techniques.what: The NY On2 right turn is set up by crossing the left foot over on count 7, then stepping forward with the right foot on count 1 while rotating the body to face forward. The key is to step INTO the turn on count 1 — not just pivot in place — so your weight placement is unambiguous. After the turn, resume the basic step: forward on 2, back on 3, then 5-6-7 core beat.

techniques.drill: Solo: mark a spot on the floor. On count 7 cross left over right, on count 1 step forward with right and land facing your original direction. Repeat 8 times. Check: did you step forward or just spin? Your right foot should land 6–8 inches ahead of where it started.
techniques.common_error: Pivoting in place on count 1 instead of stepping forward. This makes your weight ambiguous and breaks partner connection. Drive the right foot forward as you rotate.

hard_transitions.why: The core beat on 5-6-7 must fully complete with weight on left before the right foot crosses on 1. Rushing the core beat causes the cross to land early and off-timing.
Weight must end on the non-crossing foot (left) at count 3 before the left foot crosses on 5. If weight is ambiguous, the mirror cross is late and the criss-cross pattern collapses.
The right turn entry requires crossing the LEFT foot on count 7 — opposite of the Suzy Q cross. Students often cross the wrong foot because the Suzy Q pattern is still in muscle memory.
The most common error: pivoting in place on 1 instead of stepping forward. The right foot must travel forward 6-8 inches to make weight placement clear for partner connection.

drills.name: Slow Count Basic
drills.instructions: No music. Say '5-6-7, 1-2-3' aloud. On every count, transfer full weight so the free foot is light enough to lift. Feel the On2 break on counts 2 and 6. Do 8 phrases.

drills.name: Hip Walk Entry
drills.instructions: Add a smooth hip walk on 5-6-7 before each basic. Focus on grounded, fluid weight transfer. This is the setup for the Suzy Q transition.

drills.name: Tape Line Suzy Q
drills.instructions: Put tape on the floor. Practice cross-step-cross so the crossing foot always lands on or ahead of the tape. Say 'cross-step-cross' on each count. 4 reps eyes open, 4 reps eyes closed.

drills.name: Criss-Cross Pattern
drills.instructions: After Suzy Q left (counts 1-3), immediately cross left foot on 5 for mirror Suzy Q right. Repeat 8 times. Check: weight ends on non-crossing foot each time.

drills.name: Core Beat to Suzy Q
drills.instructions: Full phrase: 5-6-7 core beat (hip walk), then 1-3 Suzy Q. Add music at 70% speed. Focus on the transition — core beat must fully complete before the cross on 1.

drills.name: Cross-and-Step Isolation
drills.instructions: Mark a spot. On 7 cross left over right. On 1 step right foot forward 6-8 inches while rotating to face front. Repeat 8 times. Check: did your right foot travel forward or just pivot?

drills.name: Turn to Basic Resume
drills.instructions: After the right turn (counts 7, 1), continue: break left on 2, close on 3, then full 5-6-7 basic. Repeat the full phrase 8 times with music.

drills.name: Solo Full Sequence
drills.instructions: Basic (5-6-7, 1-2-3) -> Core Beat -> Suzy Q -> Criss-Cross Suzy Q -> Right Turn -> Resume Basic. Repeat with music at full speed.

drills.name: Partner Run-Through
drills.instructions: With a partner in open hold, run the full sequence. Leader: keep weight clear on every count. Follower: mirror the Suzy Q and respond to the right turn lead through the hand frame.

key_frames.label: Ready Position — Weight on Left
key_frames.description: Shows the starting position before 5-6-7. Weight clearly on left foot, right foot free. This is the reference for 'my weight's on my left foot' — the ground state before every phrase.

key_frames.label: Core Beat Complete
key_frames.description: 5-6-7 core beat finished, weight settled. This is the exact moment before the Suzy Q cross on 1. Freeze here to check: is your weight fully on the left? If not, the cross will be off-balance.

key_frames.label: Suzy Q — Count 1 Cross
key_frames.description: Right foot crossing over left on count 1. Shows the forward travel direction — the cross is moving toward the mirror, not sideways. Key frame for the 'travel forward' teaching point.

key_frames.label: Suzy Q — Count 3 End Position
key_frames.description: Right foot crossing back, weight ending on left. This is the critical end-of-Suzy-Q position. Weight must be on the non-crossing foot (left) to be ready for the criss-cross mirror on count 5.

key_frames.label: Criss-Cross — Mirror Cross Entry
key_frames.description: Left foot crossing over right on count 5, beginning the mirror Suzy Q. Shows the seamless transition from Suzy Q left to Suzy Q right — the criss-cross pattern in action.

key_frames.label: Right Turn — Count 7 Cross
key_frames.description: Left foot crossing over right on count 7 to set up the right turn. This is the most commonly confused moment — students cross the wrong foot. Freeze here: it's the LEFT foot crossing, not the right.

key_frames.label: Right Turn — Count 1 Step Forward
key_frames.description: Right foot stepping forward on count 1 while rotating to face front. Shows the 'step into the turn' principle — the foot travels forward, not just pivots. Critical for clear weight placement.

key_frames.label: Full Speed — Basic Step
key_frames.description: Basic step at full tempo. Shows the compact, grounded NY slot mechanics at speed — no excess movement, weight transfers clean, slot line maintained.

key_frames.label: Full Speed — Criss-Cross Suzy Q
key_frames.description: Mirror Suzy Q at full tempo. Hip styling visible, forward travel in slot maintained. Compare to slow walk-through frames to see how the mechanics compress at speed.

key_frames.label: Partner Work — Open Hold Basic
key_frames.description: Leader and follower in open hold doing basic step together. Shows the frame and connection point — leader's right hand at follower's left, both grounded, slot shared.

key_frames.label: Partner Work — Suzy Q Lead
key_frames.description: Leader initiating Suzy Q with follower. Leader's left hand raised to guide follower's styling. Shows how the forward travel of the Suzy Q is communicated through the frame.

key_frames.label: Partner Work — Right Turn Count 1
key_frames.description: Leader stepping forward on count 1 of right turn, follower completing turn. Shows the connection maintained through the hand frame during the turn — the step forward keeps the lead clear.

key_frames.label: Partner Work — Resume Basic After Turn
key_frames.description: Both dancers back in basic step after right turn. Shows the full sequence landing — slot re-established, weight grounded, ready to repeat the phrase.
